reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
This study investigates aeolian sand transport (windblown sand) under Earth’s atmospheric surface pressure (around 1000 mbar) and lower-pressure conditions (down to 50 mbar) in a pressure-controllable wind tunnel. The purpose is to come somewhat close to atmospheric-pressure conditions on the surface of Mars (typically 6-7 mbar), where aeolian sand transport is known to be ubiquitous. Unlike for high-pressure conditions, for lower-pressure conditions, another kind of bedform emerges (drag ripples). The authors are particularly interested in the aerodynamic roughness z0, a parameter that plays a crucial role in many aeolian transport and landscape evolution models. They aim to better understand the relative roles of different processes on the values of z0 (bedforms, sand transport, viscous-sublayer thickness, grain size). Based on their measurements, interpreted via models from the literature, they conclude that the effects of sand transport dominate in high-pressure conditions (Earth), whereas both sand transport and bedforms are important for lower pressures.

The novelty of this work lies in the report of measurements of z0 with systematically varied atmospheric conditions in a single experimental setup. Though they may be other measurements of z0 for low-pressure conditions from different studies, they are difficult to interpret if not carried out in the same experimental facility and protocol. This could turn out very helpful for a large range of future studies related to planetary geomorphology. Another novelty lies in their conclusion, which if true, furthers our physical understanding of aeolian sand transport.

I am, in principle, sympathetic to this study, though I have a potentially serious concern, which I would like the authors to address. I am not convinced that the authors are able to establish saturated aeolian sand transport in their wind tunnel for the lower-pressure conditions. The wind tunnel is 13 m long (they do not report the length of the actual test section). Assuming the test section is the full 13 m, this is just approximately twice the fetch length needed for establishing saturated sand transport for Earth pressure conditions. We have no good understanding of how much fetch one would need in lower-pressure atmospheric conditions, we only know it would be longer than on Earth, but by how much, we do not know. It is my personal opinion (I do not have convincing proof for that, since there is no good data) that the fetch needed to establish saturated conditions may be vastly longer than on Earth. If that was true, the effect of sand transport on z0 could be grossly underestimated in the present experiments (when compared with conditions on low-pressure planetary surfaces), thus challenging the authors’ conclusions. To be fair, similar concerns apply to literally all studies on aeolian sand transport that have ever been done using low-pressure wind tunnels, which is why I have strong doubts regarding all results that have ever been reported on the basis of low-pressure wind tunnels. I would like the authors to either present a clear refutation of my concern or PROMINENTLY highlight it as a major potential caveat of their results in their text.

In addition, I am curious if the authors could test the model by Pähtz & Tholen (Aeolian Research, 2021) and its implications on their results as an alternative to Eq. (9). This study found that many aeolian transport conditions may be dominated by the buffer layer between the viscous sublayer and the log-layer, leading to the prediction H_f \approx 30 (nu*g)^(2/3)/g (the authors may also vary the prefactor 30). Unlike the two equations discussed in the present study, this expression exhibits no grain size dependence whatsoever and a stronger dependence on the atmospheric pressure (via the kinematic viscosity), which could potentially alter the conclusions.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
I reiterate what I already stated in my initial report. This is a nice study that deserves publication in a prominent journal such as Nature Communication. However, I am not satisfied with the authors’ response to my serious concern. The authors responded to my comment on the potentially too short fetch with a small essay on the saturation length and the subscale saturation length. First, let me say that the subscale saturation length is not relevant for my comment, since my concern was about a potential strong underestimation of z0 associated with transport. The largest z0 one expects when transport is fully saturated. So, I will only discuss the authors arguments regarding the “actual” saturation length (see below).

1. I disagree with the notion that, if the test section length exceeds the saturation length, transport can be considered as saturated. The reason is twofold: First, the saturation length refers, roughly speaking, to the length sand transport needs to go back to the saturated state after a small disturbance of the saturated state. The processes governing this response may be substantially different from those that govern the transition from zero towards the saturated state. For example, in my opinion, the main limiting factor when going from zero to saturation in low-pressure conditions is to accelerate grains mobilized by wind or splash towards quasi-steady attractor trajectories. Especially the beginning of this transient process, when grains hops are small, can potentially be very slow. However, the higher a grain hops, the longer will it be exposed to the flow and the more energy it will gain during its hop, creating a positive feedback loop, making the transient process quicker and quicker the higher the grain hops. So, clearly, from this simple picture alone, there is a possibility that the saturation length (grains are already close to the final hop height) is much smaller than the fetch length. Second, even on Earth, where a saturation length of 0.5m-1m is quite well established, it can take up to 6m to reach saturation. This is because the saturation length is just a characteristic length in a differential equation, not the actual length to reach saturation. For example, see Selmani et al. (GRL, 2018, doi: 10.1002/2017GL076937).

2. Using the study by Andreotti et al. (2021), or a scaling reported therein, as a means to support that saturation was reached in the present study is inappropriate. First, Andreotti et al. reported for their 3.25m long test section that saturation was not reached if the surface pressure was below 300 mbar: “Upon decreasing P, this zone extends downwind, and below 300 hPa it encompasses the entire bed.” Second, there are a number of hints suggesting that many of their experiments might have been quite far from being saturated, as described in section 4.1 of Pahtz & Duran (JFM, 2023, doi: 10.1017/jfm.2023.343).

I am not claiming that my perspective on the matter will turn out to be true. I think there is a good chance that the authors’ experiments were indeed saturated. However, I think there is more than sufficient uncertainty in this regard to be cautious. The solution is pretty simple. Just state your interpretations and conclusions more cautiously and prominently acknowledge that your experiments might not have been fully saturated, and that you can therefore not conclusively rule out the possibility that transport-associated roughness might also dominate in low-pressure conditions.

“Aerodynamic Roughness of Rippled Beds Under Active Saltation
at Earth-to-Mars Atmospheric Pressures”
by Alvarez et al.
Unless otherwise noted, all cited line numbers refer to the revised manuscript (without changes
tracked). All reviewer comments were addressed point by point and in full, as detailed in our
responses below.
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Reviewer #1: Anonymous
---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
I reiterate what I already stated in my initial report. This is a nice study that deserves publication
in a prominent journal such as Nature Communication.
>> We are grateful for the reviewer’s support of our manuscript for publication in Nature
Communications and for their additional thoughts on the fetch required to reach flux saturation.
However, I am not satisfied with the authors’ response to my serious concern. The authors
responded to my comment on the potentially too short fetch with a small essay on the saturation
length and the subscale saturation length.
>> We regret that our previous response did not fully address the reviewer’s initial comment. The
reviewer’s detailed discussion of why they still believe saturation might not have been fully
reached makes conceptual sense, and although we still contend that multiple elements of our
experiments point toward a near-saturated sand flux (see below), we (1) recognize that our initial
discussion of saturation length fell short of addressing the concern because it inherently only
provides a conservative lower bound of the required fetch to reach saturation from zero flux, and
(2) agree that some uncertainty remains as sand fluxes were not directly measured. We addressed
these two points by (1) explicitly discussing the non-trivial relationship between saturation length
and the distance required to reach saturation from a zero-flux, (2) acknowledging that the
extrapolation relies on the assumption of saturated transport in our experiments, and (3) toned
down conclusions drawn on our extrapolations to Mars to acknowledge remaining uncertainty.
First, let me say that the subscale saturation length is not relevant for my comment, since my
concern was about a potential strong underestimation of z0 associated with transport. The largest
z0 one expects when transport is fully saturated. So, I will only discuss the authors arguments
regarding the “actual” saturation length (see below).
>> We would like to emphasize that our goal was to use two independent approaches to estimating
the “regular” saturation length (Durán et al., 2019 and Yizhaq et al., 2024), one of which relies on
the calculation of the subscale saturation length as an intermediate step (Yizhaq et al., 2024). Both
formulations for the regular 𝑙 yield similar values. No arguments were made in our response
based on the subscale saturation length alone. That said, we agree with the reviewer that these
1
calculations only partially address their question as longer distances may be needed when the flux
starts from zero.
1. I disagree with the notion that, if the test section length exceeds the saturation length, transport
can be considered as saturated. The reason is twofold: First, the saturation length refers, roughly
speaking, to the length sand transport needs to go back to the saturated state after a small
disturbance of the saturated state. The processes governing this response may be substantially
different from those that govern the transition from zero towards the saturated state. For example,
in my opinion, the main limiting factor when going from zero to saturation in low-pressure
conditions is to accelerate grains mobilized by wind or splash towards quasi-steady attractor
trajectories. Especially the beginning of this transient process, when grains hops are small, can
potentially be very slow. However, the higher a grain hops, the longer will it be exposed to the
flow and the more energy it will gain during its hop, creating a positive feedback loop, making the
transient process quicker and quicker the higher the grain hops. So, clearly, from this simple picture
alone, there is a possibility that the saturation length (grains are already close to the final hop
height) is much smaller than the fetch length. Second, even on Earth, where a saturation length of
0.5m-1m is quite well established, it can take up to 6m to reach saturation. This is because the
saturation length is just a characteristic length in a differential equation, not the actual length to
reach saturation. For example, see Selmani et al. (GRL, 2018, doi: 10.1002/2017GL076937).
>> We thank the reviewer for this clarification and for pointing us to the work of Selmani et al.,
2018. We envisioned the length required to reach saturation from a zero flux to scale with the
saturation length (and their “scaling factor” to be a function of u /u ). To a first order, this indeed
appears to be the case in the work of Selmani et al. (2018); however, it is clear that this factor is
greater than 1. Furthermore, the work of Selmani et al. (2018) was conducted at Earth pressure,
such that uncertainty remains as to how the relationship between both length scales is affected by
lower pressure conditions. We now explicitly discuss this point, cite the work of Selmani et al.
(2018), and acknowledge the uncertainty associated with the assumption that saturated transport
conditions were reached at l. 269-282.
2. Using the study by Andreotti et al. (2021), or a scaling reported therein, as a means to support
that saturation was reached in the present study is inappropriate. First, Andreotti et al. reported for
their 3.25m long test section that saturation was not reached if the surface pressure was below 300
mbar: “Upon decreasing P, this zone extends downwind, and below 300 hPa it encompasses the
entire bed.” Second, there are a number of hints suggesting that many of their experiments might
have been quite far from being saturated, as described in section 4.1 of Pahtz & Duran (JFM, 2023,
doi: 10.1017/jfm.2023.343).
>> Our reference to the Andreotti et al. (2021) study was confusing as it is not the source of the
relationship used; it was removed to avoid any ambiguity. The expression used by Andreotti et al.
(2021) to calculate ripple celerity was originally proposed in Durán et al. (2014) based on
experimental and field data as well as numerical simulations (the experimental and field data are
those of Andreotti et al., 2006 in the Physical Review Letters). The field measurements used to
calibrate that relationship were performed under saturated flux conditions (Andreotti et al., 2006).
Thus, the expression we use is not affected by the fact that Andreotti (2021)’s wind-tunnel
experiments may not have reached saturated flux conditions.
distinct instabilities and that the observed celerity of impact ripples aligns with those predicted
under transport at capacity. However, we recognize that this scaling relationship also involves a
pre-factor that could very well be affected by low-pressure conditions. Therefore, we opted to
better acknowledge that our experiments may not have reached fully saturated sediment transport
conditions and toned down our conclusions.
Another encouraging observation, which may hint at a near-saturated flux, is the good quantitative
agreement between our inverted focal-height parameter values (alpha and beta) and those of
Andreotti et al. (2004), calculated from the experiments of Rasmussen et al. (1996). However
again, we acknowledge that truly saturated flux conditions may not have been reached in those
experiments.
Our revised section on the extrapolation to Mars conditions now provides a better account of these
points, and explicitly acknowledges assumptions and uncertainties.
I am not claiming that my perspective on the matter will turn out to be true. I think there is a good
chance that the authors’ experiments were indeed saturated. However, I think there is more than
sufficient uncertainty in this regard to be cautious. The solution is pretty simple. Just state your
interpretations and conclusions more cautiously and prominently acknowledge that your
experiments might not have been fully saturated, and that you can therefore not conclusively rule
out the possibility that transport-associated roughness might also dominate in low-pressure
conditions.
>> We are thankful for the reviewer’s reiteration of this important point. It helped us give a better
account of remaining uncertainties and in doing so, strengthen our manuscript.

### Reviewer 1

This study investigates aeolian sand transport (windblown sand) under Earth’s atmospheric surface pressure (around 1000 mbar) and lower-pressure conditions (down to 50 mbar) in a pressure-controllable wind tunnel. The purpose is to come somewhat close to atmospheric-pressure conditions on the surface of Mars (typically 6-7 mbar), where aeolian sand transport is known to be ubiquitous. Unlike for high-pressure conditions, for lower-pressure conditions, another kind of bedform emerges (drag ripples). The authors are particularly interested in the aerodynamic roughness z0, a parameter that plays a crucial role in many aeolian transport and landscape evolution models. They aim to better understand the relative roles of different processes on the values of z0 (bedforms, sand transport, viscous-sublayer thickness, grain size). Based on their measurements, interpreted via models from the literature, they conclude that the effects of sand transport dominate in high-pressure conditions (Earth), whereas both sand transport and bedforms are important for lower pressures.

The novelty of this work lies in the report of measurements of z0 with systematically varied atmospheric conditions in a single experimental setup. Though they may be other measurements of z0 for low-pressure conditions from different studies, they are difficult to interpret if not carried out in the same experimental facility and protocol. This could turn out very helpful for a large range of future studies related to planetary geomorphology. Another novelty lies in their conclusion, which if true, furthers our physical understanding of aeolian sand transport.

I am, in principle, sympathetic to this study, though I have a potentially serious concern, which I would like the authors to address. I am not convinced that the authors are able to establish saturated aeolian sand transport in their wind tunnel for the lower-pressure conditions. The wind tunnel is 13 m long (they do not report the length of the actual test section). Assuming the test section is the full 13 m, this is just approximately twice the fetch length needed for establishing saturated sand transport for Earth pressure conditions. We have no good understanding of how much fetch one would need in lower-pressure atmospheric conditions, we only know it would be longer than on Earth, but by how much, we do not know. It is my personal opinion (I do not have convincing proof for that, since there is no good data) that the fetch needed to establish saturated conditions may be vastly longer than on Earth. If that was true, the effect of sand transport on z0 could be grossly underestimated in the present experiments (when compared with conditions on low-pressure planetary surfaces), thus challenging the authors’ conclusions. To be fair, similar concerns apply to literally all studies on aeolian sand transport that have ever been done using low-pressure wind tunnels, which is why I have strong doubts regarding all results that have ever been reported on the basis of low-pressure wind tunnels. I would like the authors to either present a clear refutation of my concern or PROMINENTLY highlight it as a major potential caveat of their results in their text.

In addition, I am curious if the authors could test the model by Pähtz & Tholen (Aeolian Research, 2021) and its implications on their results as an alternative to Eq. (9). This study found that many aeolian transport conditions may be dominated by the buffer layer between the viscous sublayer and the log-layer, leading to the prediction H_f \approx 30 (nu*g)^(2/3)/g (the authors may also vary the prefactor 30). Unlike the two equations discussed in the present study, this expression exhibits no grain size dependence whatsoever and a stronger dependence on the atmospheric pressure (via the kinematic viscosity), which could potentially alter the conclusions.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript presents interesting results for aeolian predictions based on wind tunnel estimations of aerodynamic roughness length at lower pressures than on Earth, and intended to be applied to Mars conditions.

Although the results are promising, their application to Mars conditions is questionable given the significant difference between the experimental setup performed in the study and the Mars atmosphere. Therefore, I suggest that this paper would deserve publication, but in a journal other than Nat. Communications. Some comments are detailed below that hopefully will be useful to the authors:

1) Lines 54 – 102, including equations 1-6 -> this should be included in the methods section and/or in the supplementary information, more than in the introduction.

2) Lines 70 – 71 -> please add references

3) Lines 93-97 -> these assumptions are questionable as they are presented.

4) Lines 131 – 136 -> this is not correct. The direct measurement of near-surface wind profiles on Mars, including determination of aerodynamic roughness length and wind friction speeds, was published in Sullivan et al. (2000)
Sullivan, R., R. Greeley, M. Kraft, G. Wilson, M. Golombek, K. Herkenhoff, J. Murphy, and P. Smith (2000), Results of the Imager for Mars Pathfinder windsock experiment, J. Geophys. Res., 105(E10), 24547–24562, doi:10.1029/1999JE001234.

5) Fig. 3 -> the x-axis should be “wind velocity, u (m/s)” instead of “vertical wind velocity, u (m/s)”

6) Line 250: this is assuming a neutral wind profile. However, the Martian atmosphere is almost never statically neutral, as assumed by Eq. 1. The authors should discuss how unstable conditions, typically present during the Martian daytime, or stable conditions during the night, influence the results presented in this paper.

7) Line 280 -> the experimental setup considers a minimum pressure of 50 mbar, which is several times greater than the atmospheric pressure on the Martian surface (~6 mbar), hence is questionable that the results presented in this study could be applicable to the Mars atmosphere.

8) Line 330: The nonlinear routine employed to fit the data to Eq. 1 should be described, including figures/tables showing the resulting fits, particularly if some of them (with low R^2) are omitted, as is stated in lines 333-334. Perhaps, the criteria should be better described.

9) Line 337: It is unclear if the uncertainty is calculated using the 2-3 groups of measurements as stated in line 335. Also, how much is the uncertainty of the parameters related to the nonlinear model?

## Your Original Review (Round 1)

### Reviewer 1

This study investigates aeolian sand transport (windblown sand) under Earth’s atmospheric surface pressure (around 1000 mbar) and lower-pressure conditions (down to 50 mbar) in a pressure-controllable wind tunnel. The purpose is to come somewhat close to atmospheric-pressure conditions on the surface of Mars (typically 6-7 mbar), where aeolian sand transport is known to be ubiquitous. Unlike for high-pressure conditions, for lower-pressure conditions, another kind of bedform emerges (drag ripples). The authors are particularly interested in the aerodynamic roughness z0, a parameter that plays a crucial role in many aeolian transport and landscape evolution models. They aim to better understand the relative roles of different processes on the values of z0 (bedforms, sand transport, viscous-sublayer thickness, grain size). Based on their measurements, interpreted via models from the literature, they conclude that the effects of sand transport dominate in high-pressure conditions (Earth), whereas both sand transport and bedforms are important for lower pressures.

The novelty of this work lies in the report of measurements of z0 with systematically varied atmospheric conditions in a single experimental setup. Though they may be other measurements of z0 for low-pressure conditions from different studies, they are difficult to interpret if not carried out in the same experimental facility and protocol. This could turn out very helpful for a large range of future studies related to planetary geomorphology. Another novelty lies in their conclusion, which if true, furthers our physical understanding of aeolian sand transport.

I am, in principle, sympathetic to this study, though I have a potentially serious concern, which I would like the authors to address. I am not convinced that the authors are able to establish saturated aeolian sand transport in their wind tunnel for the lower-pressure conditions. The wind tunnel is 13 m long (they do not report the length of the actual test section). Assuming the test section is the full 13 m, this is just approximately twice the fetch length needed for establishing saturated sand transport for Earth pressure conditions. We have no good understanding of how much fetch one would need in lower-pressure atmospheric conditions, we only know it would be longer than on Earth, but by how much, we do not know. It is my personal opinion (I do not have convincing proof for that, since there is no good data) that the fetch needed to establish saturated conditions may be vastly longer than on Earth. If that was true, the effect of sand transport on z0 could be grossly underestimated in the present experiments (when compared with conditions on low-pressure planetary surfaces), thus challenging the authors’ conclusions. To be fair, similar concerns apply to literally all studies on aeolian sand transport that have ever been done using low-pressure wind tunnels, which is why I have strong doubts regarding all results that have ever been reported on the basis of low-pressure wind tunnels. I would like the authors to either present a clear refutation of my concern or PROMINENTLY highlight it as a major potential caveat of their results in their text.

In addition, I am curious if the authors could test the model by Pähtz & Tholen (Aeolian Research, 2021) and its implications on their results as an alternative to Eq. (9). This study found that many aeolian transport conditions may be dominated by the buffer layer between the viscous sublayer and the log-layer, leading to the prediction H_f \approx 30 (nu*g)^(2/3)/g (the authors may also vary the prefactor 30). Unlike the two equations discussed in the present study, this expression exhibits no grain size dependence whatsoever and a stronger dependence on the atmospheric pressure (via the kinematic viscosity), which could potentially alter the conclusions.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript presents interesting results for aeolian predictions based on wind tunnel estimations of aerodynamic roughness length at lower pressures than on Earth, and intended to be applied to Mars conditions.

Although the results are promising, their application to Mars conditions is questionable given the significant difference between the experimental setup performed in the study and the Mars atmosphere. Therefore, I suggest that this paper would deserve publication, but in a journal other than Nat. Communications. Some comments are detailed below that hopefully will be useful to the authors:

1) Lines 54 – 102, including equations 1-6 -> this should be included in the methods section and/or in the supplementary information, more than in the introduction.

2) Lines 70 – 71 -> please add references

3) Lines 93-97 -> these assumptions are questionable as they are presented.

4) Lines 131 – 136 -> this is not correct. The direct measurement of near-surface wind profiles on Mars, including determination of aerodynamic roughness length and wind friction speeds, was published in Sullivan et al. (2000)
Sullivan, R., R. Greeley, M. Kraft, G. Wilson, M. Golombek, K. Herkenhoff, J. Murphy, and P. Smith (2000), Results of the Imager for Mars Pathfinder windsock experiment, J. Geophys. Res., 105(E10), 24547–24562, doi:10.1029/1999JE001234.

7) Line 280 -> the experimental setup considers a minimum pressure of 50 mbar, which is several times greater than the atmospheric pressure on the Martian surface (~6 mbar), hence is questionable that the results presented in this study could be applicable to the Mars atmosphere.

8) Line 330: The nonlinear routine employed to fit the data to Eq. 1 should be described, including figures/tables showing the resulting fits, particularly if some of them (with low R^2) are omitted, as is stated in lines 333-334. Perhaps, the criteria should be better described.

9) Line 337: It is unclear if the uncertainty is calculated using the 2-3 groups of measurements as stated in line 335. Also, how much is the uncertainty of the parameters related to the nonlinear model?

### Reviewer 1

I reiterate what I already stated in my initial report. This is a nice study that deserves publication in a prominent journal such as Nature Communication. However, I am not satisfied with the authors’ response to my serious concern. The authors responded to my comment on the potentially too short fetch with a small essay on the saturation length and the subscale saturation length. First, let me say that the subscale saturation length is not relevant for my comment, since my concern was about a potential strong underestimation of z0 associated with transport. The largest z0 one expects when transport is fully saturated. So, I will only discuss the authors arguments regarding the “actual” saturation length (see below).

1. I disagree with the notion that, if the test section length exceeds the saturation length, transport can be considered as saturated. The reason is twofold: First, the saturation length refers, roughly speaking, to the length sand transport needs to go back to the saturated state after a small disturbance of the saturated state. The processes governing this response may be substantially different from those that govern the transition from zero towards the saturated state. For example, in my opinion, the main limiting factor when going from zero to saturation in low-pressure conditions is to accelerate grains mobilized by wind or splash towards quasi-steady attractor trajectories. Especially the beginning of this transient process, when grains hops are small, can potentially be very slow. However, the higher a grain hops, the longer will it be exposed to the flow and the more energy it will gain during its hop, creating a positive feedback loop, making the transient process quicker and quicker the higher the grain hops. So, clearly, from this simple picture alone, there is a possibility that the saturation length (grains are already close to the final hop height) is much smaller than the fetch length. Second, even on Earth, where a saturation length of 0.5m-1m is quite well established, it can take up to 6m to reach saturation. This is because the saturation length is just a characteristic length in a differential equation, not the actual length to reach saturation. For example, see Selmani et al. (GRL, 2018, doi: 10.1002/2017GL076937).

2. Using the study by Andreotti et al. (2021), or a scaling reported therein, as a means to support that saturation was reached in the present study is inappropriate. First, Andreotti et al. reported for their 3.25m long test section that saturation was not reached if the surface pressure was below 300 mbar: “Upon decreasing P, this zone extends downwind, and below 300 hPa it encompasses the entire bed.” Second, there are a number of hints suggesting that many of their experiments might have been quite far from being saturated, as described in section 4.1 of Pahtz & Duran (JFM, 2023, doi: 10.1017/jfm.2023.343).

I am not claiming that my perspective on the matter will turn out to be true. I think there is a good chance that the authors’ experiments were indeed saturated. However, I think there is more than sufficient uncertainty in this regard to be cautious. The solution is pretty simple. Just state your interpretations and conclusions more cautiously and prominently acknowledge that your experiments might not have been fully saturated, and that you can therefore not conclusively rule out the possibility that transport-associated roughness might also dominate in low-pressure conditions.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 1

This study investigates aeolian sand transport (windblown sand) under Earth’s atmospheric surface pressure (around 1000 mbar) and lower-pressure conditions (down to 50 mbar) in a pressure-controllable wind tunnel. The purpose is to come somewhat close to atmospheric-pressure conditions on the surface of Mars (typically 6-7 mbar), where aeolian sand transport is known to be ubiquitous. Unlike for high-pressure conditions, for lower-pressure conditions, another kind of bedform emerges (drag ripples). The authors are particularly interested in the aerodynamic roughness z0, a parameter that plays a crucial role in many aeolian transport and landscape evolution models. They aim to better understand the relative roles of different processes on the values of z0 (bedforms, sand transport, viscous-sublayer thickness, grain size). Based on their measurements, interpreted via models from the literature, they conclude that the effects of sand transport dominate in high-pressure conditions (Earth), whereas both sand transport and bedforms are important for lower pressures.

The novelty of this work lies in the report of measurements of z0 with systematically varied atmospheric conditions in a single experimental setup. Though they may be other measurements of z0 for low-pressure conditions from different studies, they are difficult to interpret if not carried out in the same experimental facility and protocol. This could turn out very helpful for a large range of future studies related to planetary geomorphology. Another novelty lies in their conclusion, which if true, furthers our physical understanding of aeolian sand transport.

I am, in principle, sympathetic to this study, though I have a potentially serious concern, which I would like the authors to address. I am not convinced that the authors are able to establish saturated aeolian sand transport in their wind tunnel for the lower-pressure conditions. The wind tunnel is 13 m long (they do not report the length of the actual test section). Assuming the test section is the full 13 m, this is just approximately twice the fetch length needed for establishing saturated sand transport for Earth pressure conditions. We have no good understanding of how much fetch one would need in lower-pressure atmospheric conditions, we only know it would be longer than on Earth, but by how much, we do not know. It is my personal opinion (I do not have convincing proof for that, since there is no good data) that the fetch needed to establish saturated conditions may be vastly longer than on Earth. If that was true, the effect of sand transport on z0 could be grossly underestimated in the present experiments (when compared with conditions on low-pressure planetary surfaces), thus challenging the authors’ conclusions. To be fair, similar concerns apply to literally all studies on aeolian sand transport that have ever been done using low-pressure wind tunnels, which is why I have strong doubts regarding all results that have ever been reported on the basis of low-pressure wind tunnels. I would like the authors to either present a clear refutation of my concern or PROMINENTLY highlight it as a major potential caveat of their results in their text.

In addition, I am curious if the authors could test the model by Pähtz & Tholen (Aeolian Research, 2021) and its implications on their results as an alternative to Eq. (9). This study found that many aeolian transport conditions may be dominated by the buffer layer between the viscous sublayer and the log-layer, leading to the prediction H_f \approx 30 (nu*g)^(2/3)/g (the authors may also vary the prefactor 30). Unlike the two equations discussed in the present study, this expression exhibits no grain size dependence whatsoever and a stronger dependence on the atmospheric pressure (via the kinematic viscosity), which could potentially alter the conclusions.

### Reviewer 2

The manuscript presents interesting results for aeolian predictions based on wind tunnel estimations of aerodynamic roughness length at lower pressures than on Earth, and intended to be applied to Mars conditions.

Although the results are promising, their application to Mars conditions is questionable given the significant difference between the experimental setup performed in the study and the Mars atmosphere. Therefore, I suggest that this paper would deserve publication, but in a journal other than Nat. Communications. Some comments are detailed below that hopefully will be useful to the authors:

1) Lines 54 – 102, including equations 1-6 -> this should be included in the methods section and/or in the supplementary information, more than in the introduction.

2) Lines 70 – 71 -> please add references

3) Lines 93-97 -> these assumptions are questionable as they are presented.

4) Lines 131 – 136 -> this is not correct. The direct measurement of near-surface wind profiles on Mars, including determination of aerodynamic roughness length and wind friction speeds, was published in Sullivan et al. (2000)
Sullivan, R., R. Greeley, M. Kraft, G. Wilson, M. Golombek, K. Herkenhoff, J. Murphy, and P. Smith (2000), Results of the Imager for Mars Pathfinder windsock experiment, J. Geophys. Res., 105(E10), 24547–24562, doi:10.1029/1999JE001234.

5) Fig. 3 -> the x-axis should be “wind velocity, u (m/s)” instead of “vertical wind velocity, u (m/s)”

6) Line 250: this is assuming a neutral wind profile. However, the Martian atmosphere is almost never statically neutral, as assumed by Eq. 1. 7) Line 280 -> the experimental setup considers a minimum pressure of 50 mbar, which is several times greater than the atmospheric pressure on the Martian surface (~6 mbar), hence is questionable that the results presented in this study could be applicable to the Mars atmosphere.

8) Line 330: The nonlinear routine employed to fit the data to Eq. 1 should be described, including figures/tables showing the resulting fits, particularly if some of them (with low R^2) are omitted, as is stated in lines 333-334. Perhaps, the criteria should be better described.

9) Line 337: It is unclear if the uncertainty is calculated using the 2-3 groups of measurements as stated in line 335. Also, how much is the uncertainty of the parameters related to the nonlinear model?
